title: When To Start Enforcing Consequences
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Following up on the risk of starting consequences too early or too late, Linsin lays out three specific conditions that must be met, ideally within the first hour of the first day of school, before a teacher should begin enforcing consequences. First, explain the purpose of the plan in terms of protecting students' right to learn and enjoy class, not as being about the teacher or parents. Second, provide the facts of the plan itself — rules and consequences — in a brief 10-to-15-minute, no-frills explanation with optional light modeling. Third, make two promises to the class: that the teacher will follow the plan exactly as written, and that the teacher will never show anger when enforcing it. He argues these promises create 'soft pressure' that increases both teacher consistency and student buy-in, and closes by noting that if these three conditions are met clearly and confidently, most classes will need little to no further re-teaching of the plan itself, only routines and transitions.
points: Enforce consequences only after three specific conditions are met, ideally within the first hour of the first day of school.
Condition one is explaining the plan's purpose as protecting students' right to learn and enjoy class, explicitly not about the teacher or parents.
Condition two is a brief, fact-only explanation of rules and consequences taking 10-15 minutes, with no lengthy commentary needed.
Condition three is making two promises to the class: to follow the plan exactly as written, and to never show anger when enforcing it.
These two promises create 'soft pressure' on the teacher toward consistency while also making students like and want to please the teacher from the start.
quotes: Giving warnings and time-outs too soon can cause resentment. On the other hand, allowing a full week of grace sends the message that you don’t trust your students and their ability to follow rules.
A simple rule of thumb is that once three conditions are met you can and should begin enforcing consequences.
Your students need to know the purpose of your classroom management plan, which isn’t about you or their parents or anyone else. It’s about them and what is best for them.
This should take 10-15 minutes, no more, regardless of your grade level. There is no need for lengthy commentary or theatrical demonstration.
A second promise is to never show anger when they break a rule. You won’t scold them, lecture them, or raise your voice.

But I’ve discovered that if you’re exceptionally clear and confident while fulfilling the three conditions, and you boldly follow through as promised, there is an excellent chance your class will eagerly stay within the boundaries you’ve set.
